high_yield_pearls: ACE inhibitors block conversion of Angiotensin I → Angiotensin II.
The dry cough is caused by accumulation of bradykinin — switch to ARB if intolerable.
Angioedema is rare but life-threatening — contraindicated in patients with prior angioedema.
First-line for hypertension in patients with diabetes or CKD.
Monitor potassium — can cause hyperkalemia, especially with K+-sparing diuretics.
Contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic — causes fetal renal damage).
Beta-blockers block beta-adrenergic receptors, reducing heart rate and contractility.
Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol) block both B1 (heart) and B2 (lungs) — avoid in asthma/COPD.
Cardioselective beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol) primarily target B1 — safer in pulmonary disease.
Can mask signs of hypoglycemia (tachycardia) — use with caution in diabetics on insulin.
Never abruptly discontinue — can trigger rebound hypertension or MI.
Carvedilol is a non-selective beta-blocker + alpha-1 blocker used in heart failure.
Schedule II = high abuse potential with currently accepted medical use.
No refills allowed — requires a new written prescription each time.
Opioids (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl) act on Mu receptors — primary risk is respiratory depression.
Stimulants (amphetamine, methylphenidate) used for ADHD — risk of cardiovascular effects and abuse.
Fentanyl is 100x more potent than morphine — high overdose risk.
Naloxone (Narcan) reverses opioid overdose — keep on hand for high-risk patients.
In New York State, anabolic steroids are classified as Schedule II (stricter than federal Schedule III).
Schedule III = moderate to low physical dependence, high psychological dependence potential.
Up to 5 refills allowed within 6 months.
Acetaminophen/codeine combinations (e.g., Tylenol #3) are Schedule III federally.
Anabolic steroids are Schedule III federally — but Schedule II in New York State.
Buprenorphine (used in MAT for opioid use disorder) is Schedule III.
Ketamine is Schedule III — used for anesthesia and treatment-resistant depression.
Schedule IV = lower abuse potential than Schedule III; up to 5 refills in 6 months.
Benzodiazepines (-pam/-lam) enhance GABA-A receptor activity — CNS depression.
Avoid combining benzodiazepines with opioids — synergistic respiratory depression risk (Black Box Warning).
Benzodiazepines are high-risk in elderly patients (Beers Criteria) — increased fall and fracture risk.
Tramadol is Schedule IV — weak opioid agonist, also inhibits serotonin/NE reuptake.
Zolpidem (Ambien) is Schedule IV — non-benzo sleep aid, acts on GABA-A.
Never abruptly stop benzodiazepines — withdrawal can cause life-threatening seizures.
Schedule V = lowest abuse potential among controlled substances.
Some Schedule V products (e.g., cough syrups with <200mg codeine/100mL) may be sold OTC in some states.
Pregabalin (Lyrica) is Schedule V — used for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and seizures.
Lacosamide is Schedule V — adjunct for partial-onset seizures.
Diphenoxylate/atropine (Lomotil) is Schedule V — antidiarrheal with opioid component.
Despite low scheduling, patients can still develop dependence — monitor accordingly.
SSRIs block serotonin reuptake — mnemonic: 'Serotonin Stays Right In.'
First-line treatment for depression and anxiety disorders.
Takes 2–6 weeks for full therapeutic effect — counsel patients on delayed onset.
Serotonin syndrome risk when combined with MAOIs, tramadol, or triptans — potentially fatal.
Black box warning: increased suicidal ideation in patients under 25, especially early in treatment.
Fluoxetine has the longest half-life — least likely to cause discontinuation syndrome.
Paroxetine has the shortest half-life — highest risk of discontinuation syndrome.
